definition: Apertus is a public large language model, developed by the Swiss AI Initiative (a collaboration between EPFL, ETH Zurich, and the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre).
details: It was released on September 2, 2025, under the free and open-source Apache 2.0 license. Designed initially for business and research use cases around the world, Apertus was trained on over 1800 languages, and comes in 8 billion or 70 billion parameter versions and is available on Hugging Face for download. The model was developed aiming to adhere to European copyright law, and is one of the first examples of AI as a public good in the vein of AI sovereignty. It is also the first large model to comply with the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act. At its launch, the model creators emphasized multilinguality, transparency, and auditability as priorities in contrast to commercial frontier model. While international reception was largely positive, the first iteration was significantly behind the capabilities of frontier models and needs adaptation for many use cases with chatbots being a secondary but not a primary use case. As of late 2025, it was considered the largest and most capable fully open model. The capability of future models will depend in part on how much more funding can be secured.

explainer.lead: Apertus is a publicly released large language model built by Switzerland’s Swiss AI Initiative, with 8-billion and 70-billion-parameter versions. It matters because it pairs multilingual coverage with open access, transparency, auditability, and an explicit focus on European legal compliance rather than chasing commercial frontier-model performance alone.

tiers.eli5: Apertus is like a giant language machine in a public library: anyone can download it instead of having to rent access to a company’s private machine. It learned from text covering more than 1,800 languages and comes in a smaller and a larger size. Its first version is not as capable as the strongest commercial models, so many jobs still require extra adaptation.
tiers.practitioner: Download either the 8-billion or 70-billion-parameter version from Hugging Face, choosing between the two available sizes for business or research work. For example, a research team could obtain the 8-billion-parameter version and adapt it for a multilingual task rather than treating it as a finished chatbot. Plan for task-specific adaptation: the first iteration substantially trails frontier models, and chatbots are a secondary rather than primary use case.
tiers.paperLevel: Apertus is a public LLM with parameter count θ ∈ {8 × 10^9, 70 × 10^9}, developed by the Swiss AI Initiative and trained on more than 1,800 languages. It was released under Apache 2.0 with multilinguality, transparency, auditability, European copyright-law adherence, and EU AI Act compliance as central goals. Its initial capabilities were significantly below frontier models, many use cases require adaptation, and future capability gains depend partly on securing additional funding.

flow: Training draws on language coverage spanning more than 1,800 languages.
Users obtain a version from Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license.
Business or research teams adapt it for their use case, with chatbots treated as a secondary application.
explainer.origin: Apertus was developed by the Swiss AI Initiative, a collaboration between EPFL, ETH Zurich, and the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre. It was released on September 2, 2025, under the Apache 2.0 license.
explainer.lineage: It is an early example of AI developed as a public good in the context of AI sovereignty and the first large model to comply with the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act. By late 2025 it was considered the largest and most capable fully open model, while the capabilities of future versions depended partly on further funding.
explainer.whyItMatters: Apertus offers a public, auditable alternative to commercial frontier models, combining broad language coverage with open licensing and European regulatory goals. Its weaker initial capabilities show the trade-off: openness and compliance do not automatically deliver frontier-level performance or ready-made applications.
